sentences.text: Maiasaura was an ornithopod hadrosaurid dinosaur.
Maiasaura peeblesorum is the only known species in the extinct genus Maiasaura.
The animal reached a maximum length of about 9 meters and a mass of up to 4 metric tons, though other sources note a weight of nearly 3 tonnes.
A prominent short, solid crest between the eyes distinguishes Maiasaura from other hadrosaurids.
Maiasaura is the official state fossil of Montana.
Evidence showed Maiasaura fed its young in the nest, marking the first known instance of parental care in dinosaurs and providing the first evidence that non-avian dinosaurs fed their young.
Whole Maiasaura eggs were discovered in 1979, representing the first whole dinosaur eggs found in North America and the Western Hemisphere.
Maiasaura chicks stayed in the nest for two years.
Maiasaura babies grew very fast, doubling their length in just four weeks.
Maiasaura reached adulthood between 4 and 6 years of age.
Maiasaura was discovered in 1978 and formally described in 1979 by paleontologists Jack Horner and Bob Makela.
In 1978, paleontologist Bob Makela was contacted by Bill Clemens regarding bones found by a woman in northwestern Montana.
Dozens of nests were found at the site now known as Egg Mountain alongside Maiasaura fossils.
Maiasaura fed on plants, leaves, fruits, and seeds.
Hunter & Janis (2026) reported evidence that Maiasaura shifted from feeding on nutritious, low-fiber plants to nutritionally poor, high-fiber plants during its life.
Dental wear analysis shows juvenile Maiasaura peeblesorum had more crush wear than adults, who displayed more shear wear.
When mating, this ornithopod built a nest and laid between 18 and 30 eggs, waiting until they hatched.
Fossil evidence shows Maiasaura was ready to leave the nest and join the herd at approximately 1.5 meters long.
By the age of two, Maiasaura reached lengths of 3 meters.
Analysis of fifty individual Maiasaura tibias revealed a mortality rate of approximately 89.9% in their first year of life.

Maiasaura lived in herds and raised its young in nesting colonies where nests were packed closely together with gaps of about 7 meters. Experts believe Maiasaura lived in enormous nomadic herds that annually returned to the same nesting site due to the large number of nests and skeletons found in North America.
Mass bone beds suggest Maiasaura herds could number as many as 10,000 individuals.
Maiasaura nests were very close together, similar to modern birds, with a space of around 7 meters between them, less than the length of an adult.
Studies by Saitta et al. suggest one sex of Maiasaura was roughly 45% larger than the other based on size statistics.

Researchers suggest the eye crest may have been used in head-butting contests between males during the breeding season, a hypothesis also proposed that the crest on Maiasaura may have been used for headbutting contests between males during breeding season.
The genus Maiasaura was described by Horner and Makela in 1979.
Maiasaura peeblesorum belongs to the tribe Brachylophosaurini alongside taxa such as Acristavus, Brachylophosaurus, Ornatops, and Probrachylophosaurus.
The closest phylogenetic relative of the genus Maiasaura appears to be Brachylophosaurus.
Maiasaura lived during the late Upper Cretaceous period, approximately between 76.7 and 70.6 million years ago in the Campanian stage.
Maiasaura lived in an interior habitat.
In the Oldman Formation of Alberta, Maiasaura lived alongside ceratopsians such as Albertaceratops, Anchiceratops, Chasmosaurus, Coronosaurus, and Wendiceratops.
It has been speculated that adults may have taken turns guarding the nest.
